concepts.decision: Place each requirement, design, control, evidence, owner, exception, and risk decision in its proper stage.
concepts.definition: Coordinated stages from stakeholder need through retirement with traceable security decisions.
concepts.failureExample: A security requirement appears only after deployment, with no design trace.
concepts.label: Information System Lifecycle

concepts.decision: Elicit before design so conflicts and acceptance conditions can be resolved.
concepts.definition: Mission, business, safety, privacy, legal, operational, and risk needs expressed by accountable parties.
concepts.failureExample: An architect assumes availability expectations without consulting operations.
concepts.label: Stakeholder Requirements

concepts.decision: Use when turning broad goals into properties, threats, measures, owners, and acceptance criteria.
concepts.definition: Refinement of needs into testable, traceable, nonconflicting requirements.
concepts.failureExample: “Protect customer data” has no classification, threat, or test condition.
concepts.label: Requirements Analysis

concepts.decision: Decide before implementation and revisit after material change.
concepts.definition: Choice of trust boundaries, controls, interfaces, dependencies, and residual-risk treatment.
concepts.failureExample: A service is built before its identity and data-flow boundaries are specified.
concepts.label: Architecture Design

concepts.decision: Use approved code, libraries, baselines, reviews, and configuration evidence.
concepts.definition: Construction and configuration of the designed system under controlled change.
concepts.failureExample: A developer bypasses a design control to meet a release date.
concepts.label: Implementation

concepts.decision: Test the boundaries and failure behavior introduced when parts are combined.
concepts.definition: Connection of components, identities, interfaces, data flows, and dependencies into an operating system.
concepts.failureExample: Two secure components exchange an unauthenticated message at their interface.
concepts.label: Integration

concepts.decision: Verify stated requirements and validate the system’s effective use and outcome.
concepts.definition: Evidence activities that check conformance to requirements and suitability for intended use.
concepts.failureExample: A system passes a unit test but fails the business recovery requirement.
concepts.label: Verification Validation

concepts.decision: Require operations ownership, monitoring, access, backup, incident, and recovery readiness.
concepts.definition: Authorized transition into operation with approved configuration, readiness, rollback, and acceptance.
concepts.failureExample: A release reaches production without log routing or rollback authority.
concepts.label: Deployment

concepts.decision: Use evidence and review to keep protection effective as the system and threats change.
concepts.definition: Sustained configuration, identity, vulnerability, monitoring, backup, incident, and change control.
concepts.failureExample: A secure launch drifts into broad access after months of unreviewed changes.
concepts.label: Operations Maintenance

concepts.decision: Plan when service ends or changes so disposition and revocation are authorized and verifiable.
concepts.definition: Controlled removal of system use, access, data, keys, media, dependencies, contracts, and retained evidence.
concepts.failureExample: A retired service leaves live credentials and customer backups accessible.
concepts.label: Retirement Disposal

concepts.decision: Make only after required tests, exceptions, owners, and risk decisions are documented.
concepts.definition: Accountable decision that security evidence, residual risk, and operational readiness meet agreed criteria.
concepts.failureExample: A sponsor accepts a system without knowing an unresolved high-risk exception.
concepts.label: Security Acceptance

misconceptions.claim: Security testing at deployment is enough.
misconceptions.correction: Requirements, architecture, implementation, operations, changes, and retirement each create security decisions and evidence needs.

outcome: Identify the lifecycle activity that should produce or validate a needed security decision, control, or evidence artifact.

sections.body: Stakeholders establish mission, constraints, assets, risk tolerance, and requirements. Analysis makes requirements testable; architecture chooses trust boundaries and controls; implementation and integration realize them; verification and validation test claims; transition ensures accepted operation. Security artifacts should be traceable: a requirement connects to design, implementation, test result, owner, exception, and residual-risk decision.
keyPoints: Verification asks whether the system meets specified requirements; validation asks whether it meets intended stakeholder need.
Traceability prevents security requirements from disappearing during handoffs.
sections.title: Security decisions mature across stages

sections.body: Operations sustain configuration, identity, monitoring, vulnerability management, change control, backups, incident response, and evidence. Retirement plans data disposition, key destruction or escrow decisions, access removal, media handling, contract exit, and retained evidence. Reassess risk whenever a lifecycle change alters the system, dependencies, threat model, or legal obligations.
keyPoints: Deployment is the start of operational assurance, not the end of engineering.
Retirement must close data, identity, supplier, and evidence obligations.
sections.title: Operations and retirement preserve the security case

sections.body: Start with stakeholder needs and requirements that state security, privacy, resilience, legal, operational, and acceptance criteria. Analyze requirements for conflicts and traceability; make architectural design decisions about trust boundaries, controls, interfaces, and residual risk; implement and integrate under controlled change; verify and validate the stated requirements with evidence; transition or deploy with approved configuration, operations readiness, and rollback; sustain through monitoring, patching, access review, incident learning, and change; then retire or dispose through data handling, revocation, records, supplier, and asset processes. Each lifecycle handoff requires an accountable owner and acceptance evidence. Failures include a secure design that is never tested, a deployment without operational logging or recovery ownership, and retirement that leaves access, data, keys, or supplier obligations active.
keyPoints: State the protected property, boundary, decision owner, operating evidence, and residual failure mode.
Treat architecture controls as lifecycle commitments: configuration, monitoring, response, maintenance, and recovery determine whether the claim holds.
sections.title: Carry security evidence through every lifecycle state

summary: Security is a lifecycle responsibility from stakeholder needs through requirements, design, implementation, integration, verification, deployment, operations, maintenance, and retirement. Decisions and evidence must survive transitions between teams.

assumptions: Only entities and claims anchored in the canonical unit or explicitly labeled hypothetical scenario are used.
A highlighted path means the learner is inspecting that path; it does not assert the event occurred.
The current source is authoritative for facts; this treatment reorganizes presentation without changing canonical content.
The lesson teaches one bounded decision and does not claim to exhaust every jurisdiction, vendor implementation, architecture, attack, or exception.

learningJob.plainExplanation: Security requirements must trace through design, implementation, acceptance, operation, change, and verified retirement. Passing build tests does not assign monitoring, patching, recovery, incident, or decommissioning ownership.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: A lifecycle with an artifact and owner at every phase would add traceability; the current revealed map does so, while the opening removes most of it.
